abstract: Copper foams deposited under various conditions are characterized in an airtight three-electrode H-cell system. Compared with the smooth copper electrode, the current density obtained on the porous copper electrodes is significantly improved. Using porous copper obtained from 0.2 M CuSO4 and 1.5 M H2SO4 electrolyte with 3 Acm 2 for 30s, the CO2 reduction current density is 27 mAcm 2 at a potential of 0.97 V vs RHE in 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte (with CO2 supplied at the flow rate of 15 sccm), tripling that of the smooth copper electrode (8 mAcm ). The average pore size of the porous copper can be reduced by adding Hexadecyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) in a small amount. Besides, the preferred orientation of crystal faces changed, which may influence the selectivity of the carbon dioxide reduction product. In the flow-cell test, at constant current 10 mAcm , the CO production rate of porous copper with CTAB additive reached 11.91μmolh cm 2 and maintained a value more than 8.95 μmolh cm 2 during one-hour electrolysis, which is much higher than smooth copper, 1.38 μmolh cm .

sections.heading: Template-Free Cu Electrodeposition to Prepare Cu–MicroBrush Electrodes for Electrochemical CO2 Reduction
sections.text:
Yueyuan Gu,[a] Jindong Li,[a] Luyang Wang,[a] Mengru Xie,[a] Xu Wu,*[a] Fang Xie,[b] and Mary P. Ryan[b]
Copper foams deposited under various conditions are characterized in an airtight three-electrode H-cell system. Compared with the smooth copper electrode, the current density obtained on the porous copper electrodes is significantly improved. Using porous copper obtained from 0.2 M CuSO4 and 1.5 M H2SO4 electrolyte with 3 Acm
2 for 30s, the CO2 reduction current density is 27 mAcm 2 at a potential of 0.97 V vs RHE in 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte (with CO2 supplied at the flow rate of 15 sccm), tripling that of the smooth copper electrode (8 mAcm 2). The average pore size of the porous
copper can be reduced by adding Hexadecyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) in a small amount. Besides, the preferred orientation of crystal faces changed, which may influence the selectivity of the carbon dioxide reduction product. In the flow-cell test, at constant current 10 mAcm 2, the CO production rate of porous copper with CTAB additive reached 11.91μmolh 1cm 2 and maintained a value more than 8.95 μmolh 1cm 2 during one-hour electrolysis, which is much higher than smooth copper, 1.38 μmolh 1cm 2.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Due to the burning of fossil fuels, the CO2-induced global warming continues increasing, which is unbeneficial to the ecological environment and human health.[1,2] Besides, in the future development of energy structure, the proportion of renewable energy will inevitably increase. An energy storage system (power-to-gas) with large capacity is needed to fill the gap between the output and the use of renewable energy (such as wind power, solar power and tidal energy).[3,4] The electrochemical reduction of CO2 can convert CO2 into useful fuels, this which may reduce CO2 emissions and promote the storage of energy as well. The electrochemical reduction of CO2 can occur under normal temperature and pressure, meanwhile the selectivity of the products and the reaction rate can be controlled by simply changing the electrolysis conditions.[4–6] Many reviews summarized electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide with various aspects,[4,7–11] such as flow cells.[12–14] The use of flow cell is essential for increasing the amount of reducing products and making the catalytic transformation of CO2 closer to practical application.
Cu is the only catalyst found so far that can effectively catalyze the electrochemical reduction of CO2 into hydrocarbons.[4,15, 16] Kuhl K P used metallic copper to electrocatalytically reduce CO2 and detected 16 CO2 reduction
products, five of which were reported for the first time in the literature.[11] The faradaic efficiency of methane and ethylene was the highest. Besides, they also propose an experimental methodology for the identification and quantification of products with unprecedented accuracy. Tang W discovered that, compared to the smooth polycrystalline copper electrode, the rough polycrystalline copper electrode has a higher specific surface area for electrocatalytic reduction of CO2.
[12] Goncalves M R found that copper electrodes with different morphologies have different selectivities, the dendritic Cu mainly produces CO, CH4, and C2H4, and copper deposits with honeycomb and three-dimensional foam structures are conducive to the formation of C2 products and suppress the generation of CH4. [13] Sen S tested the performance of the porous copper nano-foam electrode for electrochemical reduction of CO2.
[14] It was found that its overpotential was about 200 mV lower than that of a smooth copper electrode. In addition, the copper foam electrodes showed better selectivity for HCOOH and suppressed the generation of CH4 and C2H4. Lu Chen explored the reduction properties of eight smooth metal electrodes and porous electrodes in CO2-saturated 30% (w/w) MEA aqueous solution. The faradaic efficiency for formate of smooth copper and porous copper was respectively 2.1% and 9.0% at 0.8 V vs RHE.[17] Recep Kas used three-dimensional porous hollow fibre copper electrodes for electrochemical CO2 reduction, in which faradaic efficiencies for CO reached 72% at 0.4 V vs RHE.[18] Monica Padilla found porous copper films synthesized by sacrificial support method favors for electroreduction of CO2 to CO, faradaic efficiency of CO obtained 38% at 1.38 V vs RHE.[19]
Here we use a simple method which was named hydrogen bubble dynamic template to get a three-dimensional porous copper foam. During this procedure, the electrodeposition of metal and the evolution of hydrogen occur simultaneously. The

In this paper, porous copper with and without CTAB additive under optimum electrodeposition conditions were used to catalyze the reduction of CO2 in the home-made flow-cell, the gas products selectivities of which were compared.

sections.heading: The influence of deposition conditions
sections.text:
Figure 1 and Figure 2 show some SEM images of electrodeposited porous copper with different deposition time. Apparently, as the deposition time increases, the sedimentary layer thickens approximately from 50 μm to 300 μm, and the diameter of the main pore on the surface of the sedimentary layer increases from 20 μm to 70 μm, which is consistent with its growth process. The farther away from the substrate, the larger the pore size, because of the coalescence of hydrogen

The electrochemical reduction of CO2 was performed on the porous copper electrodes obtained at different deposition times, as shown in Figure 3. . Compared to the smooth copper electrode, the current density obtained on the porous copper electrodes is significantly improved. With the increase of deposition time, the current density first increases and then decreases. The current density reaches the maximum when the deposition time is 30 s, 27 mAcm 2 at a potential of 0.97 V vs RHE, tripling that of the smooth copper electrode (8 mAcm 2). Combined with the morphology of the porous copper electrodes, as the deposition time increases, the deposition amount increases, and the sedimentary layer thickens, but the reduc-
tion current density dose not increase continuously. It may be because the sediment layer is too thick and the pore walls are too dense, which are not conducive to mass transfer. Besides, we can see the clearest three-dimension porous structure when the deposition time is 30 s, which is suitable for the electrochemical reduction of CO2. It is worth noting that when the potential is between 0.2 V vs RHE and 0.6 V vs RHE, the electrode with deposition time of 80 s obtained the maximum current density. The linear sweep voltammetry curves exhibit a clear reduction peak for the 3 A-80s–1.5H-0.2Cu in the range 0.2 V to 0.5 V (Figure 5a), whereas the others only give smooth current-voltage curves. The mass of porous copper increased as the deposition time increased, which may be the reason of the appearance of the little hump.
When the deposition current density is 1 Acm 2, there are still some bare polycrystalline copper substrates seen from the SEM image (see Figure S1 in the Supporting Information). A

complete three-dimensional porous structure can be obtained when the deposition current density is between 3 Acm 2 and 9 Acm 2, and the size of the main pore, the density and the dendritic structure of the pore wall are basically the same. Besides, the thickness of the sedimentary layer is thinner when the deposition current density is 9 A/cm2 (the cross-sectional view Figure S2). When the deposition current density is between 3 Acm 2 and 9 Acm 2, the reduction current densities obtained on the porous copper are close, and the double-layer capacitances are similar too (Figure S3). Shin et al. believe that the current density has no effect on the morphology of the porous copper when the current density is greater than 0.5 Acm 2.[21,26]
As the concentration of CuSO4 increases, the dendrite deposits become more compact, both the pore walls and the deposited layers becoming thicker (Figure S4). Slightly different from Shin’s conclusion that the well-defined foam structure can be obtained when the concentration of copper ions is between 0.1 M∼0.4 M,[21,26] we found when the concentration of CuSO4 is too low (0.05 M∼0.1 M), the evolution of hydrogen mainly occurs, the deposition layers are thin, the three-dimensional porous structure is not clear. When the concentration of CuSO4 is too high (0.8 M), the pore walls are too dense (Figure S5), which may be unbeneficial to mass transfer. The three-dimensional structure of porous copper obtained when the concentration of CuSO4 is between 0.2 M and 0.4 M is moderate and the CO2 reduction performance is better (Figure S6).
As the concentration of sulfuric acid increases, the pore structure becomes more regular, the pore walls is thinner, and the pore size becomes smaller and tends to be uniform (Figure S7). The three-dimensional structure of the porous copper is incomplete, when the sulfuric acid concentration is too low (0.1 M). Shin et al. think the acidity has little effect on the foam structure when it’s sufficiently high (>1.0 M H2SO4). [21] When the concentration of the sulfuric acid increases from 0.5 M to 2 M, the diameter of the main pore decreases from 40 μm to ∼30 μm, and the thickness of the sediment reduces (Figure S8). The current density of reduction increases first and
then decreases as the deposition sulfuric acid concentration increased. The porous copper shows the best reduction performance when the deposition sulfuric acid concentration is 1.5 M (Figure S9). Combined with the cross-sectional view, the severely hydrogen evolution may suppress the copper deposition when the H2SO4 concentration was 2 M, which may explain the decline in its reduction current.
The influence of additive on porous copper electrodeposition
As shown in Figure4, the average pore size of the porous copper can be reduced from 30 μm to 20 μm by adding small amount CTAB. The morphology of the pore walls changes, and the dendritic structure condenses into clusters. When the amount of CTAB added is no less than 5 mM, the copper precipitated with flocs, thus a three-dimensional porous structure cannot be formed. CTAB has a wetting effect to reduce the surface tension of the solid/liquid interface.[27] Hydrogen bubbles can easily escape from the substrate before they gather into bigger bubbles, which may decrease the pore size of the porous copper. CTAB is a cationic surfactant, too much CTAB adsorption on the copper substrate may reduce the concentration of Cu2+ around the substrate, therefore the sedimentary layer was flocculent and the substrate was partially exposed.[28]
Compared with the porous copper obtained without CTAB additive, the reduction current density becomes smaller when CTAB was added (Figure 5a). And the more CTAB is added, the smaller the reduction current density is, which corresponds to the morphology of incomplete foam structure. When the amount of CTAB added is 10 or 50 μM, the reduction current density is still lower than the porous copper without CTAB additive, although the main pore size is reduced. Under this condition, it may be influenced by the mass transfer restriction and the change of microscopic morphological (from dendritic to granular).[28]
The XRD analysis of porous copper obtained with or without CTAB was carried out. As shown in Figure 5(b), X-ray

Although identical facets are observed in both samples, the ratios of different pairs of crystal facets are different. When the CTAB is not included, the relative peak intensity at (111) is the largest, indicating that the copper film obtained without CTAB has a preferred orientation at the (111) crystal facet. With CTAB, the peak intensity at (111) decreases and the peak intensity at (220) increases. The preferred orientation of the different crystal faces may influence the selectivity of the carbon dioxide reduction product. It has been suggested that the (111) facet is energetically favourable to produce HCOOH.[29]
Reduction tests in continuous electrolyzer
As shown in Figure 6, three different electrodes were used to test its CO2 reduction performance under several cell potentials in home-made flow-cell. The reduction current density was in this order:porous copper without CTAB additive > porous copper with CTAB additive > smooth copper. This was in accordance with the results in Figure 5(a), the reduction current density decreased when CTAB was added. The main products of the three electrodes under the measured cell potentials were H2 and CO, with minimal C2H4. The faradaic efficiencies of
CH4 and C2H6 were all less than 0.1% and were skipped in Figure 6. Under the applied cell potential, the reduction products of smooth copper were almost entirely H2, with less than 1% faradaic efficiencies of CO. For porous copper without CTAB additive, the faradaic efficiency of CO was 10.85% at 2 V cell potential, and gradually decreased as the cell potential increased. For porous copper with CTAB additive, the maximum CO efficiency 8.60% was reached at 2.5 V cell potential. The CO efficiency of porous copper without CTAB additive decreased to 3.17% when the cell potential was 2.5 V. In contrast, the CO faradaic efficiency of porous copper with CTAB additive was greater than 4.98% when the cell potential was between 2 V and 3 V. The porous copper with CTAB additive was inclined to produce CO at a more negative potential which may be beneficial to improve the yield. Besides, the porous copper with CTAB additive seemed to slightly suppress the C2H4 production.
Three different electrodes were used to test its CO2 reduction performance under constant current 10 mAcm 2 for 3600 s. Figure 7(a) shows that, under the same cathodic current, the cell voltage of porous copper with or without CTAB additive is similar, which is about +0.5 V more positive than that of smooth copper. The main gas products are hydrogen for three kinds of electrodes, and the hydrogen yield is in this order smooth copper > porous copper > porous copper with

The hydrocarbons yield in smooth copper are all bellow 0.30 μmolh 1cm 2, and the CO yield decreased gradually with time, from 1.38 μmolh 1cm 2 (900 s) to 0.35 μmol/h/cm2 (3600 s). Compared to smooth copper, the yield of CO and ethane of porous copper with or without additives were improved. Among them, CO production rate of the porous copper with CTAB additive was more stable, decreasing slightly from 11.91 μmolh 1cm 2 (900 s) to 8.95 μmolh 1cm 2 (3600 s), which was similar to the CO production rate with Cu/CNTs (8.88 μmolh 1cm 2) in Guoliang Wang’s research measured at a cell voltage of 3.0 V.[30] Correspondingly, for porous copper without CTAB additive, the CO yield decreased gradually from 10.51 μmolh 1cm 2 (900 s) to 2.97 μmolh 1cm 2 (3600 s). Besides, the ethane yield of porous copper without CTAB additive was more stable, maintaining a value more than 2.13 μmolh 1cm 2 during the one-hour electrolysis process, reaching 3.88 μmolh 1cm 2, whereas the ethane yield of porous copper with CTAB decrease quickly from 2.17 μmolh 1cm 2 (900 s) to 0.99 μmolh 1cm 2 (1800 s). The faradaic efficiencies of hydrogen were almost 100% when the current density was 20 mAcm 2 and above.
Surface analysis of the porous copper with CTAB additive before and after the one-hour electrolysis was carried out using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Figure 8). One sharp Cu 2p3/2 peak at 932.2 eV and a smaller Cu 2p1/2 peak at 952.0 eV can be observed for the Cu films before and after electrolysis.[29,31] The peaks at 932.2 eV and 952.0 eV can be assigned either to Cu(0) or Cu(I) as their peak positions are very close.[31,32] Two broad peaks at 934.0 eV and 954.1 eV were observed for the Cu films after one-hour electrolysis, both overlapping with adjacent peaks. The peaks at 934.0 eV and 954.1 eV can be assigned to the Cu 2p3/2 and Cu 2p1/2, ascribed to either Cu(II) or Cu(I).[31,33] After one-hour electrolysis, the two

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text:
The effect of electrodeposition parameters on the morphology and CO2 electrocatalytic reduction performance of porous copper have been investigated. The suitable deposition conditions are deposition time and current density of 30 s and 3 Acm 2, along with electrolyte concentration of 1.5 M H2SO4 and 0.2 M CuSO4. Under this condition,the three-dimensional porous structure is complete and the pore size is moderate, thus the CO2 reduction current density can be significantly improved, tripling that of the smooth copper electrode. With a few CTAB (less than 50 μM) additive, the main pore size of the porous copper can be reduced, and the preferred orientation of crystal faces transferred from (111) to (220). At constant cathodic current 10 mAcm 2 reduction test in a home-made flow-cell, the CO and hydrocarbons productions of porous copper increased obviously, while the smooth copper produce almost only H2. The CO production rate of porous copper with CTAB additive reached 11.91μmolh 1cm 2 and maintained a value more than 8.95 μmolh 1cm 2 during one-hour electrolysis, which is more than eight times of that of smooth copper (1.38 μmolh 1cm 2). The CO production rate of porous copper without additive decreased sharply, from 10.51 μmolh 1cm 2 (900 s) to 2.97 μmolh 1cm 2 (3600 s). This study provides a simple method to change the morphology of the copper electrode and the distribution of CO2 reduction products. The use of flow-cell is essential in the future development of CO2 electrochemical reduction. How to obtain large current density and high product selectivity under low cell voltage (high current efficiency and energy efficiency) is the focus of future research.

Detailed experimental section and supporting figures including electrolyzer structure diagram, the influence of deposition current density, copper ion concentration and hydrogen ion concentration on the morphology and reduction current of porous copper are provided in the Supporting Information.
